# Friday, 7 August 2026

_Filed 04:58, 7 August 2026._

## Top story

**OpenAI has moved the frontier claim from solving benchmark questions to producing inspectable new mathematics.** On 1 August, the company released ten results generated by an internal version of Astra, its next model family, across sphere packing, coding theory, group theory, operator algebras, circuit and quantum complexity, lattice cryptography and extremal combinatorics. OpenAI says each result resolves or substantially advances a long-standing open problem; the list includes a construction of non-sofic groups, a disproof of Connes’s rigidity conjecture, a polynomial-factor hardness result for the closest-vector problem and resolutions of three Erdős problems. The successful solution searches would have cost roughly $2,000 at current Sol API rates. Humans then prepared the manuscripts with the model, after which Astra formalised every argument as a Lean certificate; the company has published the paper, the certificates and narrated reasoning walkthroughs ([OpenAI, 1 August 2026](https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/)).

That combination matters more than the number ten. A conventional model demo asks the reader to trust a polished answer and a vendor-selected score. Here, outsiders can inspect the mathematical claims and ask a proof assistant to check whether each formal argument follows from its stated premises. It does not settle novelty, significance or whether the formal statement perfectly captures the human problem, but it creates an audit trail that ordinary chatbot output lacks. OpenAI also says the mathematical arguments were generated by the system rather than retroactively attributed to human authors—a useful line in a week full of vaguer AI-assisted claims. The released package therefore separates discovery, manuscript preparation and formal verification instead of letting one glossy output stand in for all three.

For international schools, the immediate lesson is not that students should turn Astra loose on homework; the model is unreleased, and research mathematics is unusually friendly to mechanical verification. The useful curriculum distinction is between an answer, an argument and a verified argument. Physics, mathematics and computer-science teachers can now point to a live example where AI-generated work becomes more credible only after the assumptions, proof object and checking mechanism are exposed. That is a better AI-literacy frame than teaching students to admire difficult-looking output: the frontier is impressive precisely because someone can try to break it.

## Other stories

- **Europe’s AI rules have split into a live enforcement lane and a delayed school-risk lane.** The European Commission’s enforcement powers over general-purpose AI providers began on 2 August. Providers of the most advanced models must notify the AI Office; the filing route also covers serious-incident reports, safety and security frameworks, model reports and explanations from companies that have not signed the voluntary code of practice. The Commission can now enforce those duties through fines, while older models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 have until August 2027 to comply ([European Commission, enforcement milestone 2 August 2026](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/guidelines-gpai-providers)). The Commission’s guidance also distinguishes a company that makes a significant model modification, which can inherit provider duties, from one making a minor change. That boundary matters as school vendors increasingly wrap, tune and relabel foundation models. The practical school read is deliberately less dramatic: this does not suddenly certify every classroom tool or move high-risk education systems into their final compliance regime. It does, however, begin producing a more structured vendor evidence trail upstream. For an international school serving European families and using global platforms, the useful question is no longer merely whether a provider says it follows the AI Act; it is which obligation applies, from what date, and where the model report or incident route can actually be inspected.

- **Computer-science enrolment is falling while AI coursework spreads into almost every other discipline.** Associated Press reporting published on 3 August says enrolment in computer and information sciences at US four-year institutions was down more than 8% from spring 2025, alongside weaker entry-level software-developer hiring. Universities are responding by moving AI out of the specialist silo: Virginia Commonwealth University has an AI minor, Purdue has an AI graduation requirement, Ohio State has an AI-fluency requirement, Harvard is putting model mechanics, copyright and disinformation into first-year writing, Northwestern is adding an AI major and a music-and-AI certificate, and one community college has already offered a non-credit vibe-coding class ([Associated Press, 3 August 2026](https://apnews.com/article/college-major-ai-computer-science-coding-f0dca8e4f7e16297ad27c2b02adc2530)). The institutional mechanism is unusually concrete. VCU says course development that once took about eighteen months is now happening in months or weeks; Northwestern, whose computer-science faculty had already doubled during the coding boom, is trying to hire three more professors while opening access to non-majors. The signal is neither that everyone must study computer science nor that coding is over. It is that AI literacy is becoming a cross-curricular expectation before universities have settled what it contains. A high school can get ahead by defining a small common core—model limits, verification, data judgment and disclosure—then letting disciplines supply the authentic work.

- **A year-long study found two multilingual students becoming more selective with AI, not more dependent on it.** A study placed online by the journal *System* in early August followed two advanced ESL students through their first year at US universities using monthly interviews, surveys, ChatGPT histories and supporting artefacts. Author Xiao Tan reports that the students used the system to learn unfamiliar genres, build disciplinary knowledge and navigate tacit academic conventions; across the year, both became more reflective and critical in deciding when to use it while retaining ownership of their intellectual work ([*System*, August 2026](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0346251X26001302)). The paper comes from a larger five-student project but reports only two similar cases, so it is closer to a mechanism study than an outcomes trial. Two participants cannot establish an effect, and both were advanced, self-directed learners—precisely the people most likely to make a flexible tool look good. It also cannot tell us how a novice, a reluctant writer or a student under assessment pressure would behave. The value is the mechanism, not the sample size. For a multilingual international school, it suggests that disclosure rules should distinguish outsourcing ideas from using AI to decode genre, rhetoric or institutional expectations. The more interesting assessment question becomes whether a student can explain the choices and revisions across time, not whether a detector thinks a sentence sounds machine-made.

## On the radar

- **A school-policy guide entered the market yesterday.** The National Business Education Association’s AI Task Force introduced a new AI Policy and Resource Guide for Schools on 6 August, aimed at educators, administrators, technology directors and data-protection staff ([NBEA, 6 August 2026](https://nbea.org/events/EventDetails.aspx?group=&id=2057422)). The launch was paired with a practical-policy webinar rather than an impact study. The event description promises an immediately usable framework; the substance still needs reading before it earns recommendation. Watch whether it separates staff use, student use, procurement, assessment and sensitive data—or collapses them into a single acceptable-use policy, the usual sign that a guide has been written for reassurance rather than operation.

- **Google Meet notes can now capture the slide as well as the sentence.** From 3 August, Gemini’s *Take notes for me* can add screenshots of presented content to its notes document, with administrators able to allow screenshots always or only when recording is enabled; presenters receive a notification and can disable capture from the notes panel ([Google Workspace Updates, 3 August 2026](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/08/visual-screenshots-now-included-in-Google-Meet-meeting-notes.html)). This is available to Google AI Pro for Education and is rolling out gradually over as many as fifteen days. It fixes a real weakness in transcripts, but it also turns every displayed student name, draft grade or sensitive slide into a possible note artefact. The control deserves a data-classification decision, not a convenience default.

- **Drive video feedback finally has a native timecode.** Google made timestamped comments on Drive-hosted videos available to all Workspace customers on 3 August. A comment can be anchored to a point on the timeline; clicking its marker jumps directly to that moment, while replies, mentions, edits and resolution still work normally ([Google Workspace Updates, 3 August 2026](https://workspaceupdates.googleblog.com/2026/08/provide-more-clear-contextual-feedback-with-timestamped-comments-in-Google-Drive-videos.html)). The feature is available by default, with no administrator or end-user switch. That is modest but unusually classroom-ready: performance analysis, lab technique, presentations and teacher-made tutorials can now carry precise asynchronous feedback without a separate timecode sheet. Creation is web-only; mobile viewers see the comments as ordinary file-level entries.

## Sceptic's corner

The seductive headline is that an unreleased model solved ten major mathematical problems for $2,000. The careful version has four clauses. OpenAI selected the problems and the results; the model is not available for independent reproduction; humans prepared the manuscripts with the model; and Lean checks formal deductions, not whether the formalisation captures every nuance of the original research question. The price is also an inference-cost estimate for the successful searches, not the cost of training Astra, choosing the problems, discarding failures, employing expert mathematicians or turning results into publishable papers. None of those clauses makes the work trivial. Together, they stop a research release from turning into a general claim that AI now does autonomous science cheaply.

Mathematics is also the friendliest possible demonstration field. Its arguments can be converted into proof objects with binary checking in a way that a historical interpretation, a biology experiment or a school improvement claim cannot. The result therefore strengthens the case for AI in domains with hard external verification more than it strengthens the case for trusting AI everywhere. Even OpenAI’s own publication says community engagement is needed to place the work in context and develop its ideas ([OpenAI, 1 August 2026](https://openai.com/index/ten-advances-in-mathematics/)).

The staffroom sentence is: this is evidence that AI can produce original, checkable work—not evidence that difficult-looking AI work checks itself. The impressive part is not that Astra supplied an answer. It is that the release includes enough machinery for experts to disagree with it in public.
